subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the equation of locus of a point P, if the distance of P from A(3,0) is twice the distance of P from B(−3,0).

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what 'twice the distance' becomes as an equation, and name the shape the locus turns out to be.

steps.label: Take the locus point
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. 'Twice' is a ratio in words — PA:PB = 2:1 — so this is the ratio family with the numbers hidden in a sentence.
lines: Let P = (x, y) be a point on the locus.

recall.must_convey: That the moving point is named P = (x, y) and the fixed points are written down.
accept: let P be x comma y
take the locus point as P x y
P equals x comma y is on the locus
locus point ni P x y ga teesukovali
name the moving point P with coordinates x and y

steps.why: Every locus question starts the same way: the moving point gets coordinates, and the condition is then written in terms of those coordinates.
common_mistakes: Giving the moving point fixed numbers instead of (x, y).
Mixing up which points are fixed and which one moves.

steps.label: Write the given condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. Square both sides immediately. A ratio needs no isolating and no ±, which makes this the shortest answer in the chapter.

recall.must_convey: That PA = 2PB is squared to PA² = 4PB².
accept: P A equals two P B so P A squared equals four P B squared
square both sides remembering to square the two as well
twice the distance means the ratio is two to one
P A equals two P B, square chesthe four P B square
write the condition and square it

steps.why: 'Twice the distance' is a ratio, and a ratio squares in one move with no cross term — quite unlike the sum and difference families on the facing pages.
common_mistakes: Squaring to PA² = 2PB² and forgetting to square the 2.

steps.label: Substitute the distances
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both distances go in squared, with the 4 multiplying the whole of the B bracket — its y² included, which is the step most often dropped.

recall.must_convey: That both squared distances are substituted, with 4 multiplying the entire B bracket.
accept: substitute the distance formula on both sides with four outside the B bracket
put x minus three whole squared plus y squared equals four times x plus three whole squared plus y squared
expand both sides in coordinates
distance formula substitute chesi four ni whole bracket ki apply cheyyali
four multiplies the whole of the second bracket

steps.why: The 4 multiplies a bracket holding both x and y terms, so it reaches the y² as well — that is what makes the y² coefficients differ across the equals sign and leaves a circle rather than a line.
common_mistakes: Multiplying only the x-part of the right bracket by 4.
Sign slip on (x + 3)², which expands with +6x.

steps.label: Simplify to the locus
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Collect on the side that keeps the squared terms positive, then divide by 3. Equal x² and y² coefficients — a circle again, as every ratio condition gives.

lines.text: ∴ Locus of P is x² + y² + 10x + 9 = 0

recall.must_convey: That collecting and dividing by 3 gives the circle x² + y² + 10x + 9 = 0.
accept: collect everything on one side and divide by three to get x squared plus y squared plus ten x plus nine equals zero
the x squared and y squared coefficients are equal so it is a circle
bring all the terms across and take out the common three
anni terms okavaipuku teesi three tho divide cheyyali
the locus is a circle

steps.why: Any fixed ratio of distances other than 1:1 gives a circle of Apollonius, so equal x² and y² coefficients are the check that the arithmetic held.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to divide through by the common factor 3.
Collecting 9 − 36 as +27 on the wrong side.
